ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: How to run a hackathon: a practical guide
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: What this guide covers and how to use it

content.subtitle: Planning, funding and running a student hackathon in India
content.heroText: Whether you are running a 100-person campus event or a 1,000-person weekend, this guide walks through the timeline, the budget, sponsors, the venue and the day itself, with checklists you can copy.

sections.title: What is this guide?
sections.text: Organising a hackathon has a lot of moving parts: venue access, sponsors, food, hardware, judging and participant safety. This guide puts them in order, step by step, so a first-time team knows what to do and when.

callout.title: Pro Tip
callout.text: Share this guide with your co-organisers at your first planning meeting.

sections.title: How to use this guide
sections.text: Read it end to end if this is your first event, or jump to a topic from the menu or with Ctrl+K search.

checklist.text: Read the Hackathon Timeline and pick your event date
Assign functional team leads (Logistics, Tech, Sponsorship, Marketing)
Draft a first budget using the Hackathon Budgeting page

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: What is a Hackathon?
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: What happens at a hackathon and who it is for

content.subtitle: An invention marathon where passion meets rapid prototyping
content.heroText: A hackathon is an event where people team up to build something in a fixed time, usually 24 to 48 hours, then show it to judges and each other.

sections.title: The Core Philosophy
sections.text: The point is to learn by building: try a new stack, ship a working demo in a weekend, and meet people you would want to build with again. Prizes are a bonus.

sections.title: Who attends hackathons?
sections.text: You don't need to be a Computer Science major or a veteran developer! Great teams combine programmers, UI/UX designers, hardware tinkerers, project strategists, and domain specialists.

callout.title: Plan for first-timers
callout.text: Many participants at student hackathons are attending their first one. Beginner workshops and a beginner track help them finish something.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: What is Genesis?
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Who wrote this guide

content.subtitle: Hackathon partnerships in India
content.heroText: Genesis connects companies with India's student hackathon and builder community. We curate brand partnerships with independent hackathons and run our own series, Hackers Occupied.

sections.title: How we help organisers
sections.text: If you run a student hackathon, we can help bring in sponsors. Tell us about your event on the Collaborate page.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Community Values
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Safety, inclusion, and the hacker code of conduct

content.subtitle: A safe, welcoming event for everyone
content.heroText: Publish a code of conduct and enforce it. Everyone should be free from harassment regardless of gender, sexual orientation, disability, ethnicity or background.

sections.title: Enforcing the Code of Conduct
sections.text: Link the code of conduct from your website, put posters up at check-in, and name one organiser as the incident lead who can be reached at any hour of the event.

callout.title: Safety requirement
callout.text: Provide an anonymous way to report problems and a direct emergency phone number during the event.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Digital Events
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Hosting virtual and online hackathons

content.subtitle: Running a hackathon online
content.heroText: Online hackathons let people join from anywhere. Teams collaborate over chat and video, and submit online.

sections.title: Recommended Digital Tech Stack
sections.text: Use Discord for real-time team matching and voice channels, YouTube/Twitch for keynotes and ceremonies, and Devpost/HackCulture for project submissions.

sections.title: Keeping Digital Engagement High
sections.text: Online events lose people fast. Run short 15-minute mini-events (trivia, games, quizzes) and keep mentor voice channels staffed.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: In-Person Events
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Running a 24 to 48 hour event at a venue

content.subtitle: What a venue needs
content.heroText: In-person events need more planning than online ones, and they are where teams form and people come back next year.

sections.title: Venue Essentials
sections.text: Confirm overnight building access, reliable Wi-Fi, at least one power socket per participant, accessible restrooms and a quiet rest area.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Hybrid Events
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Combining physical venues with online participation

content.subtitle: The best of both worlds with dual submission tracks
content.heroText: Hybrid hackathons allow local participants to hack in person while remote participants submit and present virtually.

sections.title: Ensuring Judging Fairness
sections.text: Run separate judging queues or virtual video rooms to ensure remote teams receive equal evaluation time compared to floor expo tables.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Hackathon Timeline
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: The 6-month operational master roadmap

content.subtitle: From initial concept to post-event wrapup
content.heroText: Work back from your event date. This is a typical six-month plan for a first event.

sections.title: Phase-by-Phase Roadmap
sections.text: Tick these off as you go.

checklist.text: Month 6: Form the organising team and pick a date
Month 5: Finalize budget & launch sponsorship prospectus
Month 4: Secure venue contract & launch teaser website
Month 3: Open hacker applications & launch marketing campaign
Month 2: Confirm sponsors, judges, keynotes, and swag orders
Month 1: Send RSVPs, finalize catering, print badges & signage
Week 1: Packing run, AV dry run, mentor briefing

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Finding the Date & Purpose
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Avoiding scheduling conflicts and defining your theme

content.subtitle: Strategic scheduling for maximum attendance
content.heroText: Choosing the wrong date can destroy attendance. Cross-check university exam schedules, major holidays, and competing regional tech events before locking in your date.

sections.title: Date Selection Checklist
sections.text: Check academic calendars for midterms and finals, national holidays, local weather patterns, and major tech conference dates.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Build Your Leadership Team
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Structuring functional organising committees

content.subtitle: Give each lead clear ownership
content.heroText: Split the work into clear areas, each with one person responsible.

sections.title: Core organising areas
sections.text:
1. Lead Director (Overall vision & sync)
2. Logistics Director (Venue, catering, AV, security)
3. Sponsorship Lead (Funding, partner relations)
4. Tech & Web Lead (Platform, registration system, Wi-Fi)
5. Marketing & Design Lead (Socials, branding, swag)
6. Hacker Experience Lead (Mentors, mini-events, judging)

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Locking Down a Venue
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Facility requirements, contracts, and power setup

content.subtitle: Finding and booking a venue
content.heroText: Check overnight access approvals, ventilation and power before you sign anything.

sections.title: Power & Gigabit Networking
sections.text: A normal classroom cannot power 50 laptops from one wall. Work with the venue's facilities team on distribution boards and cables across several circuits.

callout.title: Power Rule of Thumb
callout.text: Plan for about 150 W per participant. A 300-person hackathon needs roughly 45 kW of continuous power.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Hackathon Budgeting
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Financial planning, line items, and reserve funds

content.subtitle: Planning income and costs
content.heroText: A budget agreed early stops you running out of food or money on the day. These are typical shares; adjust them for your event.

sections.title: Standard Expense Allocations
sections.text:
- Food & Beverage: 40-45%
- Swag & Shirts: 15-20%
- Travel & Logistics: 15%
- Prizes & Hardware: 10%
- Audio/Visual & Security: 10%
- Emergency Reserve: 5-10%

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Sponsorship Overview
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Fundraising strategy and tier structures

content.subtitle: Why companies sponsor hackathons
content.heroText: Sponsors fund your event to recruit top talent, drive developer adoption of their APIs/SDKs, and build brand affinity among student creators.

sections.title: What Sponsors Care About
sections.text: Tailor your pitch to what company representatives care about: HR teams want resumes and interview access; Developer Relations teams want API usage and project submissions.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Prospectus Creation
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: What to put in a sponsorship deck

content.subtitle: Crafting a clean, compelling 3-page proposal
content.heroText: Keep the deck short and specific: who comes, what a sponsor gets, and what it costs.

sections.title: Essential Deck Sections
sections.text:
1. Cover & Vision
2. Key Demographics & Past Statistics (Hackers count, schools, diversity, projects built)
3. Tier Comparison Table (Title, Gold, Silver, Bronze)
4. Custom Add-ons (Meal sponsorship, Hardware lab, Lounge naming)
5. Contact & Payment Info

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Pitching Sponsors
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Outreach campaigns, follow-ups, and closing contracts

content.subtitle: Outreach, follow-ups and closing
content.heroText: Start your outreach 4 to 6 months in advance. Target University Recruiter and Developer Advocate titles on LinkedIn.

sections.title: Outreach Best Practices
sections.text: Keep initial cold emails under 150 words. Highlight your expected hacker headcount, university reach, and unique track opportunities.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Making an Accessible Design
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: WCAG compliance, mobile UX, and high contrast

content.subtitle: Designing for every hacker on all screen sizes
content.heroText: Your website is often the first thing participants and sponsors see. Check colour contrast, labels, screen reader support and keyboard navigation.

sections.title: Accessibility Checklist
sections.text: Maintain minimum 4.5:1 text contrast ratio, provide alt text on all images, ensure all buttons have accessible labels, and support keyboard tab navigation.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Placeholder Website
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Put up a simple page early

content.subtitle: Capturing early emails before registrations open
content.heroText: Do not wait for the full site. Put up a one-page teaser with an email sign-up about five months before the event.

sections.title: Teaser Elements
sections.text: Hero headline, tentative date and city, email newsletter subscribe form, sponsor outreach contact link.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Main Website
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Full schedule, FAQs, sponsor grid, and application flow

content.subtitle: The central hub for hackers, mentors, and sponsors
content.heroText: Your main website should answer every question a participant might ask within 2 clicks.

sections.title: Essential Sections
sections.text:
- Hero Section & Register CTA
- About & Mission Statement
- Schedule & Tracks
- Prizes & Sponsor Logos
- FAQ Accordion
- Code of Conduct & Footers

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Marketing Your Event
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Social campaigns, campus ambassadors, and posters

content.subtitle: Spreading the word across tech communities
content.heroText: Combine social posts with campus ambassadors at nearby colleges.

sections.title: Campus Ambassador Playbook
sections.text: Recruit student leads at neighbouring colleges to share flyers, post on class Discord servers, and host info sessions.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Managing Registrations
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Applications, ticketing, RSVPs, and check-in flows

content.subtitle: Streamlining application reviews and attendance confirmation
content.heroText: Free events usually see a share of registered people not turn up, so accept more registrations than you have seats. Track your own drop-off rate to set the margin.

sections.title: RSVP Strategy
sections.text: Send acceptance notifications in waves. Require hackers to confirm RSVPs 7 days before the event so waitlisted applicants can be promoted.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Judging & Submissions
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Expo style judging, scoring rubrics, and platforms

content.subtitle: Fair, transparent, and efficient project evaluations
content.heroText: For large hackathons, expo-style judging (teams demo at their tables) lets every team show their project to several judges, which stage presentations cannot.

sections.title: Standard Judging Rubric
sections.text:
1. Technical Complexity (25%)
2. Design & User Experience (25%)
3. Originality & Innovation (25%)
4. Utility & Impact (25%)

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Hackathon Scheduling
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Planning a 24 to 36 hour agenda

content.subtitle: Balancing hacking time, workshops, and rest
content.heroText: Ensure long uninterrupted hacking blocks while weaving in fun mini-events and technical workshops.

sections.title: Sample 24-Hour Agenda
sections.text:
Day 1 09:00 AM - Check-in & Breakfast
Day 1 11:00 AM - Opening Ceremony
Day 1 12:00 PM - Hacking Begins & Team Building
Day 1 01:30 PM - Lunch & Sponsor Workshops
Day 1 07:00 PM - Dinner
Day 1 10:00 PM - Cup Stacking Mini-Event
Day 2 00:00 AM - Midnight Pizza & Gaming
Day 2 08:00 AM - Breakfast
Day 2 12:00 PM - Hacking Ends & Submissions Due
Day 2 01:00 PM - Science Fair Judging Expo
Day 2 04:00 PM - Closing Ceremony & Awards

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Mentorship
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Onboarding and organising technical mentors

content.subtitle: Getting teams unstuck
content.heroText: Recruit experienced engineers, alumni and sponsor developer advocates to help teams when they are stuck.

sections.title: Help Desk Ticketing
sections.text: Use a ticket queue (a Discord bot or a simple web form) where teams give their table number, stack and problem, so mentors can pick up requests in order.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Day-of Logistics & Hacker Experience
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: On-site operations, meals, swag, and emergency response

content.subtitle: Running the day itself
content.heroText: Write the run of show minute by minute, and give core staff walkie-talkies or a dedicated emergency chat channel.

sections.title: Hacker Experience Essentials
sections.text: Keep water stations full, maintain clean restrooms, hand out snacks every 4 hours, and provide earplugs/sleeping masks in designated rest areas.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: After the Event
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Post-mortems, metrics, winner follow-ups, and thank-yous

content.subtitle: Closing the loop and building community momentum
content.heroText: After the closing ceremony, thank sponsors, pay out prizes promptly and hold a team retrospective.

sections.title: Post-Event Checklist
sections.text: Send attendee survey, publish winner project showcase, distribute tax receipts to sponsors, process reimbursements, and write an internal retrospective document.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Hardware Introduction
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Why host hardware & IoT hackathons?

content.subtitle: Combining physical electronics with software intelligence
content.heroText: Hardware hackathons allow participants to build physical gadgets, robotics, wearables, and smart home IoT systems using microcontrollers and sensors.

sections.title: What Makes Hardware Special
sections.text: Hardware hackers need physical workbenches, soldering stations, component check-out counters, 3D printers, and safety gear.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Hardware Labs & Setup
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Equipment inventories, component check-out, and safety

content.subtitle: Setting up a safe hardware lab
content.heroText: Provide a diverse inventory of microcontrollers (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, ESP32), sensor kits, wire strippers, breadboards, and soldering equipment.

sections.title: Mandatory Safety Rules
sections.text: Always require safety goggles in soldering areas, provide fume extractors, maintain a first aid burn kit, and prohibit high-voltage main grid hacking without approval.

callout.title: Safety First
callout.text: Have a trained lab manager supervise soldering stations at all times.

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Templates to make
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: The planning documents every organising team needs

content.subtitle: Five documents to set up before you start
content.heroText: Most teams end up building the same few documents. Set them up early and share them with every lead.

sections.title: What to set up
sections.text:
- Budget sheet: every income and cost line, with a reserve
- Sponsorship deck: audience, packages and contact
- Run of show: the event minute by minute, with owners
- Volunteer roster: shifts and responsibilities
- Incident log: what happened, when, and what was done

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Host Exciting Mini-Events
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: Cup stacking, Slides Karaoke, Esports, and trivia ideas

content.subtitle: Short breaks that keep people going
content.heroText: Mini-events break up intense coding sessions, relieve stress, and create fun memories.

sections.title: Ideas that work
sections.text:
1. Cup Stacking Challenge (Fastest team to build a 50-cup pyramid)
2. Slides Karaoke (Hackers present random 5-slide decks they've never seen before)
3. Midnight Cupcake Decorating
4. Smash Bros / Valorant Tournament
5. Tech Trivia & Meme Contest

ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.title: Software for Hackathons
ALL_GUIDE_ARTICLES.desc: The recommended organising tech stack

content.subtitle: Tools that automate your operations
content.heroText: Use software for ticketing, team matching, chat moderation and submissions.

sections.title: Recommended Tools
sections.text:
- Project Submissions: Devpost / HackCulture
- Community & Chat: Discord / Slack
- Registration & Ticketing: Luma / Eventbrite
- Mentorship: HelpQueue / Discord Ticket Bot
- Live Stream: OBS Studio + YouTube Live

content.subtitle: An invention marathon where passion meets rapid prototyping
content.heroText: A hackathon is an event where people team up to build something in a fixed time, usually 24 to 48 hours, then show it to judges and each other.

sections.title: The Core Philosophy
sections.text: The point is to learn by building: try a new stack, ship a working demo in a weekend, and meet people you would want to build with again. Prizes are a bonus.

sections.title: Who attends hackathons?
sections.text: You don't need to be a Computer Science major or a veteran developer! Great teams combine programmers, UI/UX designers, hardware tinkerers, project strategists, and domain specialists.

callout.title: Plan for first-timers
callout.text: Many participants at student hackathons are attending their first one. Beginner workshops and a beginner track help them finish something.

articles.title: What is Genesis?
articles.desc: Who wrote this guide

content.subtitle: Hackathon partnerships in India
content.heroText: Genesis connects companies with India's student hackathon and builder community. We curate brand partnerships with independent hackathons and run our own series, Hackers Occupied.

sections.title: How we help organisers
sections.text: If you run a student hackathon, we can help bring in sponsors. Tell us about your event on the Collaborate page.

articles.title: Community Values
articles.desc: Safety, inclusion, and the hacker code of conduct

content.subtitle: A safe, welcoming event for everyone
content.heroText: Publish a code of conduct and enforce it. Everyone should be free from harassment regardless of gender, sexual orientation, disability, ethnicity or background.

sections.title: Enforcing the Code of Conduct
sections.text: Link the code of conduct from your website, put posters up at check-in, and name one organiser as the incident lead who can be reached at any hour of the event.

callout.title: Safety requirement
callout.text: Provide an anonymous way to report problems and a direct emergency phone number during the event.

articles.title: Digital Events
articles.desc: Hosting virtual and online hackathons

content.subtitle: Running a hackathon online
content.heroText: Online hackathons let people join from anywhere. Teams collaborate over chat and video, and submit online.

sections.title: Recommended Digital Tech Stack
sections.text: Use Discord for real-time team matching and voice channels, YouTube/Twitch for keynotes and ceremonies, and Devpost/HackCulture for project submissions.

sections.title: Keeping Digital Engagement High
sections.text: Online events lose people fast. Run short 15-minute mini-events (trivia, games, quizzes) and keep mentor voice channels staffed.

articles.title: In-Person Events
articles.desc: Running a 24 to 48 hour event at a venue

content.subtitle: What a venue needs
content.heroText: In-person events need more planning than online ones, and they are where teams form and people come back next year.

sections.title: Venue Essentials
sections.text: Confirm overnight building access, reliable Wi-Fi, at least one power socket per participant, accessible restrooms and a quiet rest area.

articles.title: Hybrid Events
articles.desc: Combining physical venues with online participation

content.subtitle: The best of both worlds with dual submission tracks
content.heroText: Hybrid hackathons allow local participants to hack in person while remote participants submit and present virtually.

sections.title: Ensuring Judging Fairness
sections.text: Run separate judging queues or virtual video rooms to ensure remote teams receive equal evaluation time compared to floor expo tables.

articles.title: Hackathon Timeline
articles.desc: The 6-month operational master roadmap

content.subtitle: From initial concept to post-event wrapup
content.heroText: Work back from your event date. This is a typical six-month plan for a first event.

sections.title: Phase-by-Phase Roadmap
sections.text: Tick these off as you go.

checklist.text: Month 6: Form the organising team and pick a date
Month 5: Finalize budget & launch sponsorship prospectus
Month 4: Secure venue contract & launch teaser website
Month 3: Open hacker applications & launch marketing campaign
Month 2: Confirm sponsors, judges, keynotes, and swag orders
Month 1: Send RSVPs, finalize catering, print badges & signage
Week 1: Packing run, AV dry run, mentor briefing

articles.title: Finding the Date & Purpose
articles.desc: Avoiding scheduling conflicts and defining your theme

content.subtitle: Strategic scheduling for maximum attendance
content.heroText: Choosing the wrong date can destroy attendance. Cross-check university exam schedules, major holidays, and competing regional tech events before locking in your date.

sections.title: Date Selection Checklist
sections.text: Check academic calendars for midterms and finals, national holidays, local weather patterns, and major tech conference dates.

articles.title: Build Your Leadership Team
articles.desc: Structuring functional organising committees

content.subtitle: Give each lead clear ownership
content.heroText: Split the work into clear areas, each with one person responsible.

sections.title: Core organising areas
sections.text:
1. Lead Director (Overall vision & sync)
2. Logistics Director (Venue, catering, AV, security)
3. Sponsorship Lead (Funding, partner relations)
4. Tech & Web Lead (Platform, registration system, Wi-Fi)
5. Marketing & Design Lead (Socials, branding, swag)
6. Hacker Experience Lead (Mentors, mini-events, judging)

articles.title: Locking Down a Venue
articles.desc: Facility requirements, contracts, and power setup

content.subtitle: Finding and booking a venue
content.heroText: Check overnight access approvals, ventilation and power before you sign anything.

sections.title: Power & Gigabit Networking
sections.text: A normal classroom cannot power 50 laptops from one wall. Work with the venue's facilities team on distribution boards and cables across several circuits.

callout.title: Power Rule of Thumb
callout.text: Plan for about 150 W per participant. A 300-person hackathon needs roughly 45 kW of continuous power.

articles.title: Hackathon Budgeting
articles.desc: Financial planning, line items, and reserve funds

content.subtitle: Planning income and costs
content.heroText: A budget agreed early stops you running out of food or money on the day. These are typical shares; adjust them for your event.

sections.title: Standard Expense Allocations
sections.text:
- Food & Beverage: 40-45%
- Swag & Shirts: 15-20%
- Travel & Logistics: 15%
- Prizes & Hardware: 10%
- Audio/Visual & Security: 10%
- Emergency Reserve: 5-10%

articles.title: Sponsorship Overview
articles.desc: Fundraising strategy and tier structures

content.subtitle: Why companies sponsor hackathons
content.heroText: Sponsors fund your event to recruit top talent, drive developer adoption of their APIs/SDKs, and build brand affinity among student creators.

sections.title: What Sponsors Care About
sections.text: Tailor your pitch to what company representatives care about: HR teams want resumes and interview access; Developer Relations teams want API usage and project submissions.

articles.title: Prospectus Creation
articles.desc: What to put in a sponsorship deck

content.subtitle: Crafting a clean, compelling 3-page proposal
content.heroText: Keep the deck short and specific: who comes, what a sponsor gets, and what it costs.

sections.title: Essential Deck Sections
sections.text:
1. Cover & Vision
2. Key Demographics & Past Statistics (Hackers count, schools, diversity, projects built)
3. Tier Comparison Table (Title, Gold, Silver, Bronze)
4. Custom Add-ons (Meal sponsorship, Hardware lab, Lounge naming)
5. Contact & Payment Info

articles.title: Pitching Sponsors
articles.desc: Outreach campaigns, follow-ups, and closing contracts

content.subtitle: Outreach, follow-ups and closing
content.heroText: Start your outreach 4 to 6 months in advance. Target University Recruiter and Developer Advocate titles on LinkedIn.

sections.title: Outreach Best Practices
sections.text: Keep initial cold emails under 150 words. Highlight your expected hacker headcount, university reach, and unique track opportunities.

articles.title: Making an Accessible Design
articles.desc: WCAG compliance, mobile UX, and high contrast

content.subtitle: Designing for every hacker on all screen sizes
content.heroText: Your website is often the first thing participants and sponsors see. Check colour contrast, labels, screen reader support and keyboard navigation.

sections.title: Accessibility Checklist
sections.text: Maintain minimum 4.5:1 text contrast ratio, provide alt text on all images, ensure all buttons have accessible labels, and support keyboard tab navigation.

articles.title: Placeholder Website
articles.desc: Put up a simple page early

content.subtitle: Capturing early emails before registrations open
content.heroText: Do not wait for the full site. Put up a one-page teaser with an email sign-up about five months before the event.

sections.title: Teaser Elements
sections.text: Hero headline, tentative date and city, email newsletter subscribe form, sponsor outreach contact link.

articles.title: Main Website
articles.desc: Full schedule, FAQs, sponsor grid, and application flow

content.subtitle: The central hub for hackers, mentors, and sponsors
content.heroText: Your main website should answer every question a participant might ask within 2 clicks.

sections.title: Essential Sections
sections.text:
- Hero Section & Register CTA
- About & Mission Statement
- Schedule & Tracks
- Prizes & Sponsor Logos
- FAQ Accordion
- Code of Conduct & Footers

articles.title: Marketing Your Event
articles.desc: Social campaigns, campus ambassadors, and posters

content.subtitle: Spreading the word across tech communities
content.heroText: Combine social posts with campus ambassadors at nearby colleges.

sections.title: Campus Ambassador Playbook
sections.text: Recruit student leads at neighbouring colleges to share flyers, post on class Discord servers, and host info sessions.

articles.title: Managing Registrations
articles.desc: Applications, ticketing, RSVPs, and check-in flows

content.subtitle: Streamlining application reviews and attendance confirmation
content.heroText: Free events usually see a share of registered people not turn up, so accept more registrations than you have seats. Track your own drop-off rate to set the margin.

sections.title: RSVP Strategy
sections.text: Send acceptance notifications in waves. Require hackers to confirm RSVPs 7 days before the event so waitlisted applicants can be promoted.

articles.title: Judging & Submissions
articles.desc: Expo style judging, scoring rubrics, and platforms

content.subtitle: Fair, transparent, and efficient project evaluations
content.heroText: For large hackathons, expo-style judging (teams demo at their tables) lets every team show their project to several judges, which stage presentations cannot.

sections.title: Standard Judging Rubric
sections.text:
1. Technical Complexity (25%)
2. Design & User Experience (25%)
3. Originality & Innovation (25%)
4. Utility & Impact (25%)

articles.title: Hackathon Scheduling
articles.desc: Planning a 24 to 36 hour agenda

content.subtitle: Balancing hacking time, workshops, and rest
content.heroText: Ensure long uninterrupted hacking blocks while weaving in fun mini-events and technical workshops.

sections.title: Sample 24-Hour Agenda
sections.text:
Day 1 09:00 AM - Check-in & Breakfast
Day 1 11:00 AM - Opening Ceremony
Day 1 12:00 PM - Hacking Begins & Team Building
Day 1 01:30 PM - Lunch & Sponsor Workshops
Day 1 07:00 PM - Dinner
Day 1 10:00 PM - Cup Stacking Mini-Event
Day 2 00:00 AM - Midnight Pizza & Gaming
Day 2 08:00 AM - Breakfast
Day 2 12:00 PM - Hacking Ends & Submissions Due
Day 2 01:00 PM - Science Fair Judging Expo
Day 2 04:00 PM - Closing Ceremony & Awards

articles.title: Mentorship
articles.desc: Onboarding and organising technical mentors

content.subtitle: Getting teams unstuck
content.heroText: Recruit experienced engineers, alumni and sponsor developer advocates to help teams when they are stuck.

sections.title: Help Desk Ticketing
sections.text: Use a ticket queue (a Discord bot or a simple web form) where teams give their table number, stack and problem, so mentors can pick up requests in order.

articles.title: Day-of Logistics & Hacker Experience
articles.desc: On-site operations, meals, swag, and emergency response

content.subtitle: Running the day itself
content.heroText: Write the run of show minute by minute, and give core staff walkie-talkies or a dedicated emergency chat channel.

sections.title: Hacker Experience Essentials
sections.text: Keep water stations full, maintain clean restrooms, hand out snacks every 4 hours, and provide earplugs/sleeping masks in designated rest areas.

articles.title: After the Event
articles.desc: Post-mortems, metrics, winner follow-ups, and thank-yous

content.subtitle: Closing the loop and building community momentum
content.heroText: After the closing ceremony, thank sponsors, pay out prizes promptly and hold a team retrospective.

sections.title: Post-Event Checklist
sections.text: Send attendee survey, publish winner project showcase, distribute tax receipts to sponsors, process reimbursements, and write an internal retrospective document.

articles.title: Hardware Introduction
articles.desc: Why host hardware & IoT hackathons?

content.subtitle: Combining physical electronics with software intelligence
content.heroText: Hardware hackathons allow participants to build physical gadgets, robotics, wearables, and smart home IoT systems using microcontrollers and sensors.

sections.title: What Makes Hardware Special
sections.text: Hardware hackers need physical workbenches, soldering stations, component check-out counters, 3D printers, and safety gear.

articles.title: Hardware Labs & Setup
articles.desc: Equipment inventories, component check-out, and safety

content.subtitle: Setting up a safe hardware lab
content.heroText: Provide a diverse inventory of microcontrollers (Arduino, Raspberry Pi, ESP32), sensor kits, wire strippers, breadboards, and soldering equipment.

sections.title: Mandatory Safety Rules
sections.text: Always require safety goggles in soldering areas, provide fume extractors, maintain a first aid burn kit, and prohibit high-voltage main grid hacking without approval.

callout.title: Safety First
callout.text: Have a trained lab manager supervise soldering stations at all times.

articles.title: Templates to make
articles.desc: The planning documents every organising team needs

content.subtitle: Five documents to set up before you start
content.heroText: Most teams end up building the same few documents. Set them up early and share them with every lead.

sections.title: What to set up
sections.text:
- Budget sheet: every income and cost line, with a reserve
- Sponsorship deck: audience, packages and contact
- Run of show: the event minute by minute, with owners
- Volunteer roster: shifts and responsibilities
- Incident log: what happened, when, and what was done

articles.title: Host Exciting Mini-Events
articles.desc: Cup stacking, Slides Karaoke, Esports, and trivia ideas

content.subtitle: Short breaks that keep people going
content.heroText: Mini-events break up intense coding sessions, relieve stress, and create fun memories.

sections.title: Ideas that work
sections.text:
1. Cup Stacking Challenge (Fastest team to build a 50-cup pyramid)
2. Slides Karaoke (Hackers present random 5-slide decks they've never seen before)
3. Midnight Cupcake Decorating
4. Smash Bros / Valorant Tournament
5. Tech Trivia & Meme Contest

articles.title: Software for Hackathons
articles.desc: The recommended organising tech stack

content.subtitle: Tools that automate your operations
content.heroText: Use software for ticketing, team matching, chat moderation and submissions.

sections.title: Recommended Tools
sections.text:

- Community & Chat: Discord / Slack
- Registration & Ticketing: Luma / Eventbrite
- Mentorship: HelpQueue / Discord Ticket Bot
- Live Stream: OBS Studio + YouTube Live

## How we run events.
The rules we hold ourselves to when we run a hackathon or partner on one. Hold us to them.

### Our six rules

#### Working builds over slides
Judges at events we run score what a team built during the event. A demo that works beats a polished pitch deck.

#### Build in public
We encourage teams to share their code, write up what broke, and keep their projects online after the event.

#### Open to anyone who builds
You do not need a computer science degree or a famous college. First-timers, designers and self-taught developers are welcome at every event we run.

#### Numbers we can back up
We only publish figures we can source, and we say when a number is a projection rather than a result.

#### Help each other
Mentors, organisers and other teams are there to get you unstuck. Asking early is encouraged.

#### Leave it better
We respect venues, mentors' time and other people's work, and we clean up after ourselves.
At every event

### Code of conduct

#### Credit other people's work
Name the libraries, APIs and teammates you used. Submitting someone else's work as your own is not allowed.

#### Critique the work, not the person
Challenge ideas and code directly, and stay kind to the people behind them.

#### Say when you do not know
Nobody knows everything at 3 AM. Asking is how teams finish.

#### No harassment, ever
Harassment, discrimination and gatekeeping are not tolerated at any Genesis event, online or offline.

#### Report a problem
At an event, tell any organiser straight away. Afterwards, email
[link] partner@genesishacks.com → mailto:partner@genesishacks.com

### Who we are
Genesis Hacks (“Genesis”, “we”, “us”) runs the website at www.genesishacks.com. Genesis connects companies with India's student hackathon and builder community. We curate brand partnerships with independent hackathons and run our own series, Hackers Occupied.
For the purposes of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (the “DPDP Act”), Genesis Hacks decides why and how the personal data described here is used, so we are the Data Fiduciary for it. You are the Data Principal.
The short version.
We collect what you type into our forms so we can reply to you, we never sell it, analytics stay off unless you accept them, and you can ask us to see, correct or delete your data at any time by writing to
[link] partner@genesishacks.com → mailto:partner@genesishacks.com
.

### What we collect, form by form
We only collect what each form asks for. Fields marked optional on a form can be left empty.
Personal data collected by each form
| Form | What it collects | Why |
| Contact (home page and /contact) | Name, email, who you are reaching out as, your message | To reply to you |
| Partner or sponsor (/partner) | Name, email, phone or WhatsApp (optional), company or college, website, partnership type, goals, event of interest, budget band, timeline, your message, and an optional deck (PDF or PowerPoint, up to 3 MB) | To understand and answer a sponsorship or partnership enquiry |
| Collaborate (/collaborate) | Name, email, phone or WhatsApp (optional), organisation or event, type of collaboration, website, your message | To discuss co-hosting, judging, mentoring or listing your event |
| Join the crew (/careers) | Name, email, phone, the area you want to work in, experience, portfolio link, your message | To consider you for volunteer or paid work at our events |
| Hackers Occupied Delhi interest (/events/hackers-occupied-delhi) | Name, email, phone, college or organisation, city, tracks you care about, whether you have a team | To tell you when registration for Hackers Occupied Delhi opens |
| Certificates (/certificates/hackers-occupied-pune) | The email and phone you registered with | To check them against the participant list and issue your certificate. We do not keep a copy of what you type |

#### Collected automatically
- Security and spam control. When you send a form we store a one-way, salted hash of your IP address and your browser’s user agent, so we can block repeated or automated submissions. We cannot turn the hash back into your IP address.
- Server logs. Our hosting provider keeps short-lived technical logs (IP address, time, page requested) to run and protect the site.
- Analytics, only with your consent. If you click Accept on the cookie banner, PostHog records the pages you visit, device type, approximate region and where you came from. If you click Reject, or do nothing, no analytics load.
We do not ask for sensitive information such as financial details, health data or identity documents through this site. Please do not include them in a message or upload.

### Why we use it, and on what basis
We use your personal data to:
- reply to your message or enquiry and keep the conversation going;
- assess sponsorship, partnership and collaboration requests and match them to events;
- tell you about the event you registered interest in, such as Hackers Occupied Delhi;
- consider crew applications;
- issue certificates to registered participants;
- keep the site secure and free of spam; and
- with your consent, understand which pages are useful.
Consent. Sending a form is a clear, affirmative act: you give us your data for the purpose shown on that form. Analytics run only on your separate consent through the cookie banner.
Legitimate uses. Some processing relies on the legitimate uses allowed by section 7 of the DPDP Act, for example using data you gave us voluntarily for the purpose you gave it, or keeping records a law requires us to keep.
We do not sell personal data, we do not use it for advertising, and we do not make automated decisions about you.

### Who we share it with
A small number of service providers (Data Processors) handle data on our behalf, under contract and only to provide their service to us:
Service providers that process personal data for Genesis Hacks
| Provider | What it does for us | Note |
| Vercel | Hosts the website and runs the server functions that receive forms | May process data outside India |
| Supabase | Database and private file storage for form submissions and uploaded decks | May process data outside India |
| Google (Workspace, Sheets, Drive) | Team email and a working copy of form submissions | May process data outside India |
| Hostinger | Hosts the mailbox for partner@genesishacks.com | Email provider for our domain |
| Resend | Sends the team a notification email when a form arrives (if enabled) | May process data outside India |
| PostHog | Optional analytics, only after you click Accept | May process data outside India |
Some of these providers store data outside India. The DPDP Act allows this unless the Government of India restricts transfers to a particular country, and we will follow any such restriction.
We share your details with a sponsor or event partner only when you ask us to (for example, to make an introduction) or when you agreed to it on an event’s own registration form. If you register for an event on another platform, such as HackCulture or Luma, that platform’s privacy policy applies to the data you give it.
We may also disclose data if the law requires it, or to protect our rights or someone’s safety.

### How long we keep it
- Enquiries (contact, partner, collaborate, crew applications, event interest): up to 24 months after our last exchange with you, then deleted.
- Uploaded decks and files: up to 12 months, then deleted.
- Certificate checks: not stored. The participant list itself is kept as one-way hashes of each registered email and phone pair.
- Analytics: kept by PostHog in line with its retention settings, and only if you accepted.
We delete data sooner if you ask us to and no law requires us to keep it, or once the purpose you gave it for is complete.

### Your rights
Under the DPDP Act you can:
- ask for a summary of the personal data we hold about you and how we use it;
- ask us to correct, complete or update it;
- ask us to erase it;
- withdraw your consent at any time;
- have a grievance about our handling of your data addressed; and
- nominate another person to exercise these rights for you if you die or become unable to.
To use any of these rights, email
[link] partner@genesishacks.com → mailto:partner@genesishacks.com?subject=Data%20request
with the subject “Data request”. We reply
within 2 business days
. We may ask you to confirm it is really you before we act.
If you are not satisfied with our response, you can complain to the Data Protection Board of India.

### Withdrawing consent and cookies
Withdrawing consent is as easy as giving it. Use Cookie settings at the bottom of any page to change your analytics choice, or email us to withdraw consent for anything else. Withdrawal does not affect processing that already happened.
The site stores a few small items in your browser:
- Your consent choice (essential), so we remember whether you accepted or rejected analytics.
- Intro seen (essential, this browser session only), so the opening animation plays once.
- PostHog cookies and storage, only after you click Accept.

### Children’s data
The DPDP Act treats anyone under 18 as a child, and processing a child’s data needs verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian.
